risk.rationale: SupportBot is a customer-facing LLM chatbot (OpenAI gpt-4o-mini) that answers customer questions about orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs and hands over to a human agent on request. It interacts directly with people, so Art. 50(1) transparency applies (users must be told they are talking to an AI). It generates free-text synthetic answers, so Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking applies; the code has an open TODO (SUP-88) to label AI-generated replies, which is a compliance gap to close. It is not high-risk: the purpose is informational customer support, it makes no decisions about people, and it does not fall within any Annex III area (no credit scoring, insurance pricing, employment, education, or law enforcement use). None of the Art. 5 prohibited practices apply. The keyword pre-classifier's "limited" result is consistent with the evidence.
triggers: Art. 50(1): chatbot interacting directly with natural persons (customer support widget)
Art. 50(2): generative AI producing synthetic text replies (labelling pending, SUP-88)
Not Annex III: no credit scoring, insurance, employment, education, or law-enforcement use; no decisions about people

requirements.title: No prohibited AI practices
requirements.statement: The system does not implement any practice prohibited by Art. 5(1): subliminal or manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime prediction based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in the workplace or in education, or biometric categorisation inferring sensitive traits.

checks.description: no emotion recognition / social scoring / face scraping code

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code or documentation showing the system infers emotions (e.g. from video interviews or voice) of employees/candidates/students, scores people on social behaviour, scrapes facial images, or categorises people by biometrics into sensitive traits. A comment or doc stating that such a feature is NOT implemented is evidence of compliance, not a violation. Mark non_compliant only if a prohibited practice is actually implemented or planned for production.

requirements.title: Risk classification documented
requirements.statement: The provider documents the AI Act risk classification of the system with its rationale: the applicable Annex III area/point if high-risk, the Art. 6(3) assessment if an Annex III system is claimed not to be high-risk, or why the system is limited/minimal risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a README section, ADR or compliance document that states the risk tier AND gives a reason (e.g. "Annex III point 4(a) recruitment", "chatbot, transparency obligations under Art. 50", "spam filtering, no Annex III use case"). A bare marketing claim ("fully compliant") is not a classification.

requirements.title: Risk management system documented
requirements.statement: A risk management process is documented for the high-risk system: known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights are identified and evaluated, and targeted mitigation measures with residual-risk acceptance are recorded and kept up to date.

checks.description: a risk assessment / risk register document exists

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a risk register / risk assessment / model risk management document listing concrete risks (e.g. discrimination, automation bias, data drift), their likelihood/impact and mitigations. A single sentence like "risks are low" is not sufficient (partial at most).

requirements.title: Training data documented (datasheet)
requirements.statement: Training, validation and test data sets are documented: origin and collection process, original purpose for personal data, preparation steps (labelling, cleaning, enrichment), assumptions, and the availability/quantity/suitability of the data.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a datasheet / data card / training-data document. Code that loads a CSV is not documentation. Partial if only some of origin, preparation and splits are described.

requirements.title: Bias examination and mitigation of data sets
requirements.statement: The data sets have been examined for possible biases likely to lead to discrimination (including representativeness for the persons and setting the system is used on), and measures to detect, prevent and mitigate the identified biases are documented with results.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires an actual bias/fairness analysis with results (metrics per group, findings, mitigations). A plan ("bias audit planned"), a TODO, or merely excluding protected attributes from the features does NOT satisfy this requirement on its own (proxies may remain). Judge from documents and evaluation code/reports.

requirements.title: Technical documentation (Annex IV)
requirements.statement: Technical documentation covering the Annex IV elements exists before deployment: general description and intended purpose, versions, how the system interacts with other software, development methods, design specifications and key design choices, system architecture, and validation/testing procedures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a document (or set of docs) covers most Annex IV(1)-(2) elements. An architecture overview plus a model card without development/validation information is partial.

requirements.title: Model card for the deployed model
requirements.statement: A model card documents the deployed model: intended use and out-of-scope uses, version, training data summary, evaluation results, capabilities and known limitations.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that a model card exists and covers intended use, limitations and evaluation results.

requirements.title: Instructions for use for deployers
requirements.statement: Instructions for use are provided to deployers and contain at least: provider identity and contact, intended purpose, level of accuracy and its metrics, known limitations and foreseeable misuse risks, human oversight measures, and how to collect and interpret the logs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if the instructions contain all the listed elements. If a guide exists but misses accuracy metrics, limitations or log interpretation, the status is partial. Sections marked TBD count as missing.

requirements.title: Interpretable outputs for deployers
requirements.statement: The system provides information that lets deployers interpret each output (e.g. main reasons, feature contributions, reason codes or confidence) rather than a bare score.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that returns explanations/reason codes alongside the score and shows them to the human reviewer. A global feature-importance chart in a notebook alone is partial.

requirements.title: Disclosure of interaction with an AI system
requirements.statement: Natural persons interacting directly with the AI system (e.g. a chatbot) are informed, clearly and at the latest at the first interaction, that they are interacting with an AI system.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for user-facing UI strings (React/HTML templates, chat greeting) that tell users they talk to an AI, shown at the start of the conversation. A statement buried in terms of service is not sufficient.
evidence_queries: you are chatting with an AI

requirements.title: Marking of AI-generated content
requirements.statement: Synthetic text, image, audio or video generated by the system is marked as AI-generated in a machine-readable format (and labelled for the recipient where it is published or delivered).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that adds an AI-generated flag/header/metadata or visible label to each generated message. A TODO or ticket reference to add labelling later means non_compliant. A disclosure that the user talks to an AI (Art. 50(1)) is a different obligation and does not mark the content.

requirements.title: Affected persons informed about high-risk AI use
requirements.statement: Natural persons subject to decisions made or assisted by the high-risk AI system (candidates, applicants, workers) are informed that such a system is used on them.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a candidate/applicant notice, privacy notice or e-mail template that tells the person an AI system is used to assess them. Recruiter-facing UI text does not inform the candidate.

requirements.title: Automatic logging of AI decisions
requirements.statement: The system automatically records an event for each decision/output over its lifetime, with timestamp, input reference, output, model version and (where applicable) the human reviewer, enabling traceability and post-market monitoring.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that writes a structured record for every prediction (custom journal/audit classes count). Commented-out logging calls, TODOs or debug prints do not count. Logging only errors is not decision logging.

requirements.title: Logs retained for at least six months
requirements.statement: Automatically generated decision logs are retained for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months (>= 180 days).
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the effective retention of the decision/audit logs (config, Terraform log group, lifecycle rules). Compliant only if >= 180 days. If logs exist but retention is shorter or unbounded deletion is configured, non_compliant. If no logs exist at all, non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human can override or disregard the AI output
requirements.statement: Natural persons overseeing the system can decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse an individual output of the system, and the override is recorded.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented mechanism (API endpoint, UI action, workflow state) letting a human change the outcome. A flag set to False, a README promise without code, or an override limited to admins for model config does not count.

requirements.title: Stop / interrupt mechanism
requirements.statement: Operators can interrupt the system (a 'stop' button, kill switch or similar procedure) so that it halts in a safe state, e.g. automated processing is suspended and cases fall back to manual handling.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept any implemented switch (feature flag, admin endpoint, config) that stops automated decisions and routes work to humans. Infrastructure scaling to zero without a documented procedure is partial.

requirements.title: No adverse decision solely on the AI output
requirements.statement: Decisions adverse to natural persons (e.g. rejection, decline) are not taken automatically on the basis of the AI output alone; a competent human reviews and confirms them, mitigating automation bias.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace the decision flow in code. If any adverse outcome is set without a human step (e.g. score below threshold -> rejected), it is non_compliant; if only a subset of cases gets human review (e.g. above an amount threshold), partial.

requirements.title: Accuracy levels and metrics declared
requirements.statement: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics (e.g. AUC, precision/recall, error rates) are declared in the documentation accompanying the system (instructions for use and/or model card).
requirements.llm_guidance: Metrics must be declared in documentation shipped with the system, with values. A training script that prints accuracy is not a declaration.

requirements.title: Resilience to errors (fallback / fail-safe)
requirements.statement: The system handles errors, faults and model unavailability safely (e.g. timeouts and exceptions lead to a fail-safe outcome such as routing to manual handling, never to an automatic adverse decision).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for explicit error handling around model inference with a safe fallback. Generic web framework error pages are not sufficient.

requirements.title: Input validation against malformed or adversarial inputs
requirements.statement: Inputs to the model are validated (schema, types, ranges, size limits, file types) before inference to resist malformed or adversarial inputs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for schema validation (pydantic/zod/marshmallow), constraints and upload limits on the inference path. Reading raw request bodies directly into the model is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Protection of model endpoints against unauthorised use
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints are protected against unauthorised third parties (authentication and authorisation), so that the system's use, outputs or performance cannot be altered by exploiting vulnerabilities.
requirements.llm_guidance: Every inference and admin route must require authentication; admin/model routes need authorisation. Partial if some sensitive routes are unauthenticated.

requirements.title: Quality management and post-market monitoring procedures
requirements.statement: Documented procedures cover change management of the model/system, validation before release, post-market monitoring of performance in production (e.g. drift), and serious-incident reporting.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if the repository documents change management, pre-release validation, production monitoring AND incident reporting; partial if only some are covered.

requirements.title: Testing against predefined metrics before release
requirements.statement: The system is tested before release against prior defined metrics and thresholds appropriate to its intended purpose (e.g. an automated quality gate failing the build below a minimum AUC).
requirements.llm_guidance: Smoke tests that only check an HTTP 200 are not model validation; require assertions against metric thresholds on held-out data.

requirements.title: Lawful basis documented for each processing purpose
requirements.statement: Each purpose for which personal data is processed has a documented lawful basis under Art. 6(1) (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests), and consent is collected and recorded where it is the basis relied on.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a privacy notice, record of processing or DPIA naming the lawful basis per purpose. A README claim "fully GDPR compliant" is not evidence of a lawful basis.

requirements.title: Privacy notice provided to data subjects
requirements.statement: Data subjects receive a privacy notice at collection stating the controller and contact details, purposes and lawful basis, recipients, retention period, and their rights (access, rectification, erasure, objection, complaint).
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if a notice covering controller, purposes, legal basis, retention and rights exists and is shown/linked to data subjects. Partial if key items (e.g. retention or rights) are missing.
evidence_queries: how long we keep your data

requirements.title: Storage limitation enforced
requirements.statement: Personal data is kept no longer than necessary for its purpose: a retention period proportionate to the purpose is defined for each data category and enforced automatically (TTL, purge job, lifecycle rule).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check both that a retention period is defined AND enforced in code/IaC, and that it is proportionate (e.g. keeping raw support chats for years without justification is excessive; keeping data "forever" is non_compliant). Defined and enforced but disproportionate -> partial.

requirements.title: Right to erasure implemented
requirements.statement: A mechanism exists to erase a data subject's personal data on request without undue delay (endpoint, admin job or documented procedure covering all stores, including derived data).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented deletion path for a single data subject. Automatic expiry of all data after N days is not an on-request erasure mechanism (partial at most).

requirements.title: Safeguards for solely automated decisions
requirements.statement: Decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects are not based solely on automated processing, or, where an Art. 22(2) exception applies, the data subject can obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if no significant decision is fully automated, OR if automated decisions come with an implemented contest/appeal path leading to human review. Non_compliant if decisions are fully automated with no recourse.

requirements.title: Meaningful information about the logic involved
requirements.statement: Data subjects are informed of the existence of automated decision-making/profiling and receive meaningful information about the logic involved and its envisaged consequences.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an applicant/candidate-facing explanation of the main factors used and the consequences. Internal model documentation does not inform data subjects.

requirements.title: Data minimisation and privacy by design
requirements.statement: Only personal data necessary for the purpose is collected and used (no unnecessary sensitive or protected attributes as model features), and privacy-by-design measures such as pseudonymisation or redaction are applied before processing or sharing with third parties.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect model features and data flows. Using gender/age/nationality as features, or sending raw personal data to a third-party LLM without redaction, is non_compliant. Look for explicit redaction/pseudonymisation code.

requirements.title: Encryption of personal data at rest and in transit
requirements.statement: Personal data is encrypted at rest (databases, object storage, volumes, backups) and in transit (TLS) as appropriate to the risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at-rest and in-transit encryption must be evidenced for all stores holding personal data. Only one of the two -> partial. Self-signed dev certificates in docker-compose do not count for production.

requirements.title: Access control to personal data
requirements.statement: Access to personal data and to administrative functions is restricted to authenticated and authorised personnel (authentication, role-based authorisation, least privilege).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that endpoints exposing personal data require authentication and that admin/export routes check roles. Unauthenticated upload/listing endpoints are non_compliant.

requirements.title: Record of processing activities
requirements.statement: A record of processing activities is maintained for the system listing purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients, transfers, retention limits and security measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a ROPA entry in the repo (markdown/yaml). A DPIA or privacy notice alone is not a ROPA but may be partial if it contains the Art. 30(1) items.

requirements.title: Data protection impact assessment
requirements.statement: A DPIA has been carried out for the processing (systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing) and contains a description of the processing, necessity and proportionality assessment, risk assessment and mitigation measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a DPIA document with the Art. 35(7) elements exists.

requirements.title: AI use disclosed in user interfaces
requirements.statement: Every interface where a person interacts with the AI system or sees an AI-produced score, ranking, classification or text visibly discloses AI involvement; decision-support UIs state that the output is an AI recommendation and who decides.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect UI components, e-mail templates and notification texts. Neutral names like "Smart Score" do not disclose AI involvement.

requirements.title: AI-generated content labelled
requirements.statement: AI-generated text/media delivered to customers carries a visible "AI-generated" label and, where feasible, a machine-readable marker.
requirements.llm_guidance: A banner saying the user chats with an AI is POL-1, not POL-2. Look for per-message labelling or metadata. TODO comments do not count.

requirements.title: Prediction logging with 180-day retention
requirements.statement: Every production prediction/response is logged with timestamp, correlation id, model version, input reference and output, in tamper-resistant storage retained for at least 180 days.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both parts are needed: structured per-prediction logging AND >= 180 days retention. Logging with shorter retention -> partial. No logging -> non_compliant.
evidence_queries: prediction log model version request id

requirements.title: Raw personal-data inputs deleted within 30 days
requirements.statement: Raw inputs containing personal data (documents, messages, transcripts, payloads) are automatically deleted or anonymised within 30 days, unless a documented legal retention obligation applies.
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the retention of each raw-input store. Any raw store kept > 30 days without a documented legal obligation is non_compliant; no automated deletion at all is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Encryption at rest and TLS in transit
requirements.statement: Storage of personal data, model artefacts and logs is encrypted at rest, and all service traffic uses TLS 1.2+.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at rest and in transit must be shown; one of the two -> partial.

requirements.title: Access control on model endpoints
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints require authentication (or are declared public and rate-limited), and administrative endpoints enforce role-based authorisation.
requirements.llm_guidance: Enumerate routes. Any undeclared unauthenticated inference/upload route, or an admin route without a role check, is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human approval of adverse decisions
requirements.statement: Adverse decisions about natural persons (rejection, decline, closure) are approved by a human reviewer who sees the AI output and reasons and can change the outcome, and the approval is logged.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace adverse outcomes in code. Human approval for only part of the cases (e.g. above an amount threshold) is partial. Automatic rejection is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Model card for every deployed model
requirements.statement: Each deployed model (including third-party models) has a model card covering intended and out-of-scope use, version, training data summary, evaluation metrics, limitations and owner.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check presence and completeness of the model card(s) against the listed fields.

requirements.title: Rate limiting on AI endpoints
requirements.statement: AI endpoints reachable from untrusted networks enforce per-client rate limiting configured in code or configuration.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for rate-limit middleware (express-rate-limit, slowapi), gateway throttling or ingress annotations. Public endpoints without it are non_compliant.

requirements.title: AI incident response procedure
requirements.statement: The repository contains an AI incident response procedure (detection, escalation, reporting) that requires reporting serious incidents to the AI Governance Board within 24 hours.
requirements.llm_guidance: A generic ops runbook without AI incidents or without the 24h governance reporting is partial.

requirements.title: Bias and fairness evaluation before release
requirements.statement: A documented bias and fairness evaluation (metrics and results per protected group, mitigations) exists for the released model and is referenced from the model card.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires actual results. "Planned", TODOs or excluding protected features only is non_compliant.

verdicts.rationale: The system is a customer-support chatbot that answers questions on orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs (E1, E3). None of the excerpts show emotion inference, social scoring, facial image scraping, crime prediction, biometric categorisation, or manipulative or vulnerability-exploiting techniques. The system prompt limits the model to help-centre answers and handover (E6), and the chat widget discloses that the user is talking to an AI (E5). The evidence is about the system's declared purpose and code paths, not a formal Art. 5 assessment, and the excerpts are truncated, so confidence is moderate.
gaps: No documented Art. 5(1) prohibited-practices screening or sign-off in the repository
Excerpts are truncated; no full-repo search confirming absence of emotion, biometric or scraping code
verdicts.remediation: Add a short docs/ai-act/prohibited-practices.md (or a section in the model card) that explicitly states SupportBot does not perform emotion recognition, social scoring, biometric categorisation, facial scraping, or manipulative/vulnerability-exploiting techniques, with a dated owner sign-off. Re-run the deterministic emotion/scoring/face-scraping checks over the full repository and record the result.

verdicts.rationale: The README classifies SupportBot as a limited-risk system and gives the reason: it is a customer-facing chatbot that does not take decisions about people, is not in any Annex III area, and therefore carries Art. 50 transparency obligations (E1). The model card supports this by scoping out complaints decisions, legal, financial and contract matters and limiting use to answering questions and handing over to a human (E2). Both elements of the statement, the tier and its rationale, are evidenced. The rationale is brief and does not walk through specific Annex III points such as energy-sector critical infrastructure, but the statement does not require that depth.
gaps: No explicit screening against Annex III point 2 (energy critical infrastructure) or point 5 (essential services eligibility) is recorded
Classification is a short README paragraph rather than a dedicated, dated assessment document
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add a short docs/ai-act-classification.md (or ADR) that records the date, the owner, the Annex III points screened (including point 2 energy and point 5 essential services) and the conclusion that the system is limited-risk under Art. 50, and link it from the README "AI Act position" section.

The statement requires that users interacting directly with the AI are told, clearly and at the latest at first interaction, that they are interacting with an AI. E1 shows the chat widget header renders a visible disclosure ("You are chatting with an AI assistant...") as part of the component's initial markup, before the first bot greeting and any user message, so it is shown at the start of the conversation and is not buried in terms of service. E3 (privacy notice) and E2 (README) corroborate the AI nature of the assistant, but they are supporting documents only; the in-UI disclosure in E1 is the evidence that satisfies the requirement. No element of the statement is missing in the excerpts.
verdicts.remediation: No remediation required for this requirement. Optionally keep the disclosure string under test coverage so it is not removed in future widget changes.

verdicts.rationale: The statement requires each synthetic text output to be marked as AI-generated in a machine-readable form and labelled for the recipient. In E1, the `answer()` function returns the LLM text with no AI-generated flag, header or metadata; the `Reply` type carries only text, model, handover and usage. The only labelling reference is a TODO (SUP-88) deferring the label, which the guidance treats as non_compliant. E4 shows a chat-level notice that the user is talking to an AI, but that is the Art. 50(1) interaction disclosure and does not mark individual generated messages. The deterministic pattern match is a false positive caused by the TODO comment text in E1.
gaps: No machine-readable AI-generated marker on generated replies in server/src/llm.ts or the API response
No per-message visible AI-generated label in the chat widget (only a general chat-level disclosure)
Labelling deferred via TODO(SUP-88) rather than implemented
No metadata (e.g. provenance or generator fields) attached to stored or delivered bot messages
verdicts.remediation: 1) In server/src/llm.ts, extend the Reply type and answer() return value with machine-readable provenance, e.g. aiGenerated: true, generator: model id, and generatedAt, and expose it in the /api/chat response (for example as JSON fields plus an X-AI-Generated: true response header). 2) In server/src/transcripts.ts, persist the flag on bot messages so it survives in exports. 3) In web/src/components/ChatWidget.tsx, render a visible "AI-generated" label on each bot message, using the flag from the API. 4) Resolve TODO(SUP-88) in code rather than deferring it, and add tests asserting that every bot reply carries the marker and label. 5) Document the marking scheme in docs/ (e.g. an ADR) and reference Art. 50(2) and the exemption analysis.

The statement requires a documented Art. 6(1) lawful basis for each processing purpose, and consent recorded where consent is the basis. E1 is a privacy notice that names a basis for each purpose: supporting the customer request is under Art. 6(1)(b) (contract), and answer quality improvement and complaint handling are under Art. 6(1)(f) (legitimate interest). E2 (RoPA PA-CC-07) lists the same three purposes (customer support, quality assurance, complaint handling) and maps them to the same recipients and data, which corroborates the purpose set. Consent is not relied on for any purpose, so the consent-recording element does not apply. The legitimate-interest basis is stated but no balancing assessment is in the excerpts. The statement does not expressly require one, so this does not change the status.
gaps: No legitimate interests assessment (balancing test) visible for the Art. 6(1)(f) purpose (not required by the statement, noted for reviewer)
RoPA entry PA-CC-07 does not cross-reference the lawful basis per purpose
verdicts.remediation: Add a lawful-basis column to the RoPA entry PA-CC-07 mapping each purpose (customer support: Art. 6(1)(b); quality assurance and complaint handling: Art. 6(1)(f)) to docs/privacy.md. Optionally file a short legitimate interests assessment for the quality-assurance and complaint-handling purpose and link it from docs/ropa.md.

verdicts.rationale: Each element of the statement is evidenced. E1 names the controller with address and DPO contact, states purposes with Art. 6(1)(b) and 6(1)(f) bases, lists recipients (OpenAI as processor and the customer-care team), gives a 2-year transcript retention period, and lists access, rectification, erasure, objection and complaint rights. E2 (RoPA) is consistent on controller, purposes, recipients and retention. E4 shows the notice to users in the chat widget at the point of collection, with a link to /privacy#support-chat. The statement does not require withdrawal, portability or automated decision-making content, so their absence is not assessed here.
verdicts.remediation: No remediation is required for the elements in this statement. Optionally, keep docs/privacy.md and the RoPA entry in sync when the retention period or recipients change.

verdicts.rationale: A retention period is defined for chat transcripts (config/app.yaml sets transcript_days: 730, E4), and the ROPA records the same 2-year limit with a stated purpose (QA and complaint handling, E6). Enforcement is partly evidenced: transcripts.ts defines startRetentionJob, which runs a nightly DELETE of transcript_messages older than the configured days (E1). However, the excerpt is cut off before the job's interval and body are fully visible, and E3 imports startRetentionJob without showing where it is scheduled, so the automatic invocation is not verified. The chat_sessions table, which holds customer-linked data, has no retention period or purge anywhere in the evidence (E1 only deletes it on an erasure request). Log retention (90 days, E9/E4) is defined but is configured in the sink, not enforced in code. The 730-day period for free-text messages that may contain contact and contract data is justified in the documentation but is long, so proportionality is arguable.
gaps: No retention period or purge defined for the chat_sessions table (customer-linked data)
Automatic invocation/scheduling of startRetentionJob not visible in the evidence (E3 imports it but the call is not shown)
No documented necessity assessment for the 730-day transcript period given free-text personal data
Retention for the customer/session identifiers stored outside transcripts is not defined per data category
Log retention (90 days) is set only in the external Loki sink config; no enforcement artefact in the repo
verdicts.remediation: 1) Add a retention_days (or chat_sessions_days) setting in config/app.yaml for chat_sessions and extend the nightly purge in server/src/transcripts.ts to delete expired chat_sessions rows. 2) Show the scheduling call (e.g. startRetentionJob(cfg.retention.transcript_days) in server/src/index.ts or a worker entrypoint) and add a test or CI check that verifies the purge runs. 3) Document in docs/ropa.md or a retention policy doc why 730 days is necessary for QA and complaints, or shorten the period, and consider redacting or shortening retention for contact details in transcripts. 4) Add infra or sink config (Loki retention) as versioned IaC so the 90-day log limit is enforced from the repository.

verdicts.rationale: A single-subject deletion path exists: deleteCustomerData removes transcript_messages and chat_sessions by customer_id (E1), and E3 imports it alongside the admin transcript export. E5 states that support-admin access is required for erasure, which suggests an admin erasure route, but the route body is truncated in E3, so it is not confirmed here. Coverage is incomplete for "all stores including derived data": LLM call logs keep session_id and are only expired after 90 days, not erased on request (E12, E9, E4), and RDS backups are retained for 7 days (E13) with no documented handling. No erasure procedure document exists; the privacy notice only lists the right (E2).
gaps: No confirmed admin/API erasure endpoint wired to deleteCustomerData in the visible code
Application logs containing session_id are not erased on request; only 90-day expiry
RDS backup retention (7 days) not addressed in erasure handling
No documented erasure procedure or SLA covering all stores and the OpenAI processor
Derived data (logs, processor copies) not covered by the deletion path
verdicts.remediation: 1) Add or confirm a DELETE /admin/customers/:customerId route in server/src/index.ts guarded by requireAdmin that calls deleteCustomerData and writes an audit record. 2) Extend deleteCustomerData to cover any other stores holding customer identifiers. 3) Document in docs/erasure-procedure.md the store-by-store erasure steps: transcripts, chat_sessions, logs (redact or document expiry for session_id), RDS backups (expiry window), and OpenAI processor handling, with an undue-delay target. 4) Add an erasure section to docs/privacy.md and the ROPA entry PA-CC-07. 5) Add a test that verifies erasure removes all rows for a customer.

The statement requires privacy-by-design measures such as pseudonymisation or redaction to be applied before processing or sharing with third parties. The evidence shows raw chat text is sent to the OpenAI processor as typed, and redaction was explicitly evaluated and postponed (E4). The transcript store also keeps full message text including possible e-mail, phone and address (E7), and the RoPA lists contact data in free text (E2). No redaction or pseudonymisation code appears in the request path (E6). Some minimisation is evidenced: no sensitive attributes appear as model features (E3, E6), and retention limits exist (E5, E7, E2). Those do not cure the missing pre-processing redaction, so the requirement is not met.
gaps: No redaction or pseudonymisation of contact/contract data before sending to the third-party LLM
Redaction evaluated in ADR 0001 but deferred with no privacy-by-design alternative
Full raw message text stored in transcript_messages without redaction or pseudonymisation
No documented DPIA or necessity assessment for unredacted free-text processing
verdicts.remediation: Add a PII redaction/pseudonymisation step in server/src/llm.ts before client.chat.completions.create (e.g., detect and replace e-mail, phone, postal address, IBAN and contract numbers with reversible tokens restored only in the reply). Apply the same redaction before appendMessage in server/src/transcripts.ts, or store a pseudonymised copy alongside the raw text. Replace customer_id in logs with a keyed hash. Revise docs/adr/0001-llm-provider.md to record the redaction design and why delivery-question quality is preserved (evaluate with the 600-conversation set). Update docs/ropa.md and docs/privacy.md to describe the redaction, and add a DPIA covering unredacted processing until it ships.

verdicts.rationale: At rest, the transcript database is evidenced as encrypted: the RDS instance sets storage_encrypted=true with a customer-managed KMS key that has rotation enabled (E1), and the ROPA lists KMS-encrypted RDS as a security measure (E2). In transit, the public /api/chat ingress has a TLS secret and ssl-redirect enabled (E3), the database enforces SSL via the postgres16-force-ssl parameter group (E1), and the Postgres client sets ssl rejectUnauthorized: true (E8). Both elements are evidenced for the main store holding personal data. Coverage of other stores (application logs, backups, volumes) is not explicitly shown, which lowers confidence but is not a demonstrated failure.
gaps: No explicit evidence that application logs (90-day retention per E2) are encrypted at rest
Backup encryption is not stated explicitly, only implied by the encrypted RDS instance
Transport encryption for the outbound call to the OpenAI API is not shown in the excerpts
verdicts.remediation: Document in the infrastructure that RDS snapshots and backups use the same KMS key, and add the log store (for example CloudWatch Logs or a log bucket) with KMS encryption in Terraform. Add a short note or config showing the OpenAI client uses HTTPS only, and add it to the security section of the ROPA or an infrastructure doc.

verdicts.rationale: Authentication and role checks are evidenced. The chat endpoint requires a signed session token via sessionAuth, which returns 401 otherwise (E1, E6). The transcript export route is guarded by requireAdmin, which verifies an RS256 SSO token and requires the support-admin role (E1, E6), and E2 records admin RBAC. However, least privilege is only partly shown: a single support-admin role appears to gate both transcript export and erasure, and no finer-grained roles are evidenced (E1). Other administrative functions, such as toggling the chat.ai_enabled flag described in E5, have no visible access control. The E6 excerpt is truncated, so the erasure route's guard is not visible; E1's comment claims it is protected but the route itself is not shown.
gaps: No evidence of access control on administrative functions other than transcript export (e.g. feature flag toggle chat.ai_enabled in E5)
Least privilege not demonstrated: one broad support-admin role covers both export and erasure
Erasure route guard not visible in the excerpt (E6 truncated), only asserted in a comment in E1
No evidence of access logging or periodic review of admin role assignments
verdicts.remediation: Add an explicit authorisation check to every administrative route, including the feature-flag toggle for chat.ai_enabled, and show it in code. Split support-admin into narrower roles (e.g. transcript-read, transcript-erase, flag-admin) and enforce them per route. Confirm in server/src/index.ts that the DELETE/erasure route uses requireAdmin with the appropriate role. Log admin access to personal data (who, when, which customerId) and document the role-assignment review process in docs/ropa.md or a new access-control policy.

verdicts.rationale: The ROPA entry in docs/ropa.md (E1) covers each element the statement names: purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients (customer-care team and OpenAI Ireland as processor), transfers (none outside the EEA), erasure time limits (transcripts 2 years, logs 90 days), and security measures (TLS, KMS-encrypted RDS, admin RBAC, rate limiting). It also gives the controller and DPO contact details required by Art. 30(1)(a). The retention and security claims are consistent with the configuration: config/app.yaml sets transcript_days 730 and logging retention 90 (E9), and infra/terraform/db.tf shows storage encryption with a KMS key and a private, non-public database (E10). The privacy notice (E3) matches the ROPA on purposes, recipients and retention.
verdicts.remediation: No remediation required for this requirement. Keep docs/ropa.md updated when purposes, recipients, transfers, retention values in config/app.yaml, or the infrastructure in infra/ change.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

The one AI-facing user interface in the evidence, the chat widget, visibly discloses AI involvement in its header before any interaction: "You are chatting with an AI assistant" (E2). The disclosure is plain visible text, not a tooltip or a terms-of-service reference, and the opening bot greeting follows it. The privacy notice also states that replies come from an AI assistant and that a human agent can be requested (E3, E4). No staff-facing decision-support output (score, ranking or classification) appears in the evidence, so the POL-1(2) decision-support element has no evidenced interface to test. The TODO in E1 about labelling generated replies (SUP-88) is a note, not a control, but the widget disclosure covers the interface-level requirement.
gaps: No e-mail templates or notification texts were in the excerpts, so 'every interface' cannot be fully confirmed
No staff-facing decision-support UI is evidenced, so the who-decides statement cannot be verified where it would apply
API documentation for external integrators was not in the excerpts
verdicts.remediation: Confirm that no e-mail or notification template carries AI-generated text without an AI label, and add one where it does. Document in the repo whether any AI output reaches staff, and if so add a UI statement that the output is an AI-generated recommendation and that a named human role takes the final decision. Close SUP-88 by adding a visible AI-generated label to bot replies in ChatWidget.tsx. Add an AI-use note to any external API documentation for integrators.

verdicts.rationale: The statement requires a visible "AI-generated" label on AI-generated replies delivered to customers. The only visible disclosure in E2 is a session-level banner ("You are chatting with an AI assistant") in the widget header, which the guidance classes as POL-1 rather than per-content labelling. Bot messages are rendered in E2 as plain `<li>` items with no label. E1 shows the reply text returned without any marker, and the labelling is deferred in a TODO (SUP-88), which does not count. No machine-readable marker (header, metadata field or content credential) appears in the delivered reply; the `model_version` field in E10 and E8 is internal logging, not a marker delivered to customers. The "where feasible" qualifier applies only to the machine-readable marker, and the visible label element is clearly missing.
gaps: No per-message visible 'AI-generated' label on bot replies in ChatWidget
Labelling of AI replies deferred (TODO SUP-88), not implemented
No machine-readable marker (response header or metadata field) on chat replies returned to customers
No 'ai-generated' or 'x-ai-generated' marker found in the delivered reply path
verdicts.remediation: 1) In web/src/components/ChatWidget.tsx, render a visible "AI-generated" badge or label next to each bot message (for example inside the `<li>` for `m.from === "bot"`), and keep the session banner as an additional disclosure. 2) In the server chat route that calls answer() in server/src/llm.ts, add a machine-readable marker to every reply, such as an `X-AI-Generated: true` response header and a `generated_by: "ai"` field in the JSON body returned by sendMessage. 3) Resolve TODO(SUP-88) by removing the TODO once the badge and marker ship. 4) Add a unit or component test asserting that every bot message renders the label and that the API response carries the marker.

verdicts.rationale: Structured per-prediction logging exists: logLlmCall emits one JSON line per LLM call with a sessionId as correlation reference, model_version, and a pino timestamp, and the log lines show these fields in practice (E1, E2, E3). However, the log line carries no input reference (no input hash or record id) and no output, only token counts, latency and a handover flag, so those statement elements are not evidenced in the prediction log. Retention is configured at logging.retention_days: 90 for the Loki sink (E5), which is below the 180-day minimum, so the statement's retention element is demonstrably insufficient; the 730-day transcript retention in E5/E8 covers a different store and does not fix the log retention. No evidence of tamper-resistant (append-only/WORM) storage for the Loki logs was found, and the transcript table is mutable (DELETE statements in E8). Per the guidance, logging with shorter retention is partial.
gaps: prediction log retention is 90 days, below the 180-day minimum
no input reference (hash or record id) in the per-prediction log entry
no output recorded in the per-prediction log entry
no evidence of tamper-resistant or append-only storage for the Loki prediction logs
transcript store is mutable (DELETE/purge), not tamper-resistant
verdicts.remediation: 1) Set logging.retention_days to at least 180 in config/app.yaml and make the Loki/object-storage retention config match (e.g. retention_period 4320h or longer). 2) Extend logLlmCall in server/src/logging.ts to include an input hash or record id (e.g. SHA-256 of the prompt/message) and an output reference (hash or transcript message id) alongside the existing sessionId, model_version and timestamp. 3) Store prediction logs in append-only or WORM storage (e.g. Loki with object-lock on the S3 bucket, or a hash-chained log), and document this in docs/ with the infra/ Terraform. 4) If any retention shorter than 180 days is intended, document a formal waiver per POL-3(2).

verdicts.rationale: The raw store holding free-text customer messages (transcript_messages) is retained for 730 days (E5 transcript_days: 730), and the ROPA and privacy notice confirm a two-year erasure period (E3, E7). The nightly purge job in E1 is automated, so the deletion mechanism exists, but its window is two years, not 30 days. The only stated justification is quality assurance and complaint handling under legitimate interest (E7), which is not a documented legal retention obligation, so the statement's exception does not apply. The raw inputs therefore remain for far longer than the 30-day limit.
gaps: Transcript retention is 730 days, not at most 30 days
No documented legal retention obligation justifying the 2-year period (only QA/complaint handling under legitimate interest)
No anonymisation or redaction of raw message content after 30 days
No deterministic evidence of a <=30-day retention setting for raw inputs (deterministic check expects present)
verdicts.remediation: Set retention.transcript_days in config/app.yaml to 30 or less, or anonymise/null the content column of transcript_messages after 30 days while keeping only what QA needs. Keep the automated purge in startRetentionJob and make sure it runs with the new value. If a genuine statutory retention duty exists for part of the data (e.g. complaint or billing records), document that specific legal obligation in docs/ropa.md and a retention schedule, and limit the retained data to that scope. Update docs/privacy.md and the ROPA entry PA-CC-07 so the stated retention matches the implemented one. Consider redacting contact details before storage (ADR 0001 notes redaction was postponed), which would reduce the personal data held.

verdicts.rationale: At rest, the transcript store is evidenced: the RDS instance sets storage_encrypted = true with a customer-managed KMS key (E1), and the ROPA records KMS-encrypted RDS (E2). Nothing evidences encryption at rest for the logs, which are shipped to Loki (E10) and written to a local log file (E7), or for model artefacts. In transit, the public /api/chat ingress terminates TLS with an ssl-redirect (E3), and the DB parameter group is named postgres16-force-ssl (E1). However, no excerpt shows the minimum TLS version (1.2+) or TLS for traffic between internal services, and the parameter group contents are not shown.
gaps: No evidence of encryption at rest for the Loki log store or the application log files
No evidence of encryption at rest for model artefacts or prediction-log storage
No explicit TLS 1.2 minimum enforced on the ingress or load balancer
No evidence of TLS for traffic between internal services
The force-SSL setting of the DB parameter group is implied by its name but not shown in the excerpts
verdicts.remediation: Add IaC or config showing encryption at rest for the logging backend (Loki/object storage with a KMS key) and for any artefact or log buckets. Document where model artefacts are stored, or state that none are stored locally. Set an explicit TLS 1.2 minimum in the ingress (e.g. nginx ssl-protocols "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3") and show the postgres16-force-ssl parameter values. Add mTLS or TLS configuration for service-to-service traffic, and record the TLS policy in docs/security.md.

verdicts.rationale: The only inference route, POST /api/chat, is declared in config/app.yaml as public (E3, referenced by the comment in E2), is rate-limited by chatLimiter (E2, E3), and is gated by sessionAuth, which rejects requests without a valid signed session token (E1). The only visible administrative route, GET /admin/transcripts/:customerId, uses requireAdmin, which verifies an SSO RS256 token and requires the support-admin role, returning 403 otherwise (E1, E2). No model-reload or threshold-change endpoints appear in the excerpts, and index.ts is cut off at line 44, so the route inventory is not fully visible; truncation alone is not treated as a gap.
gaps: Full route inventory not visible: index.ts excerpt ends at line 44
No model-reload or threshold-change endpoints evidenced; cannot confirm they are absent or protected
Chat rate-limit key uses the client-supplied x-session-id header, which a client can vary
verdicts.remediation: Provide the complete server/src/index.ts (or a generated route list) to confirm every route is either behind sessionAuth/requireAdmin or declared in public_endpoints. If model-management routes (reload, threshold changes, export) exist, protect them with requireAdmin. Consider keying the rate limiter on the verified session id or IP rather than the client-supplied header.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

A model card exists at MODEL_CARD.md (E1) and covers the owner, intended use, out-of-scope uses, product-level evaluation metrics and limitations for the deployed third-party model OpenAI gpt-4o-mini. The card has no training data summary for the provider model; the only data description is the retrieval corpus in E4, which is grounding rather than training data. Version is only weakly evidenced in the card: it names the alias pinned via LLM_MODEL (E1, E10), while the concrete snapshot gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 appears only in runtime logs (E6).
gaps: No training data summary for the third-party model (gpt-4o-mini) in the model card
Model card does not record the concrete pinned model version/snapshot; only the alias 'gpt-4o-mini' is stated
verdicts.remediation: Update MODEL_CARD.md to add a 'Training data summary' section that cites the provider's published training-data description for gpt-4o-mini and states that no fine-tuning is done (per docs/adr/0001-llm-provider.md), plus a note on the retrieval corpus (help-centre extracts). Record the exact pinned version (e.g. gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18) in the card and pin that snapshot in config/app.yaml and the LLM_MODEL default instead of the floating alias.

verdicts.rationale: The public endpoint /api/chat is declared in config/app.yaml (E1) and exposed through a public ingress (E5). E3 applies express-rate-limit middleware (dependency in E6) to POST /api/chat, with a per-minute limit read from configuration (cfg.rate_limit.chat_per_minute = 20 in E1) and a per-client key (session header, falling back to IP). E8 shows the limiter firing in production ("rate limit exceeded"). The main weakness is that the key uses the unverified client-supplied x-session-id header, so a client can rotate it to evade the limit; the statement's "session or IP" wording still permits this keying, so it does not change the status but should be hardened.
gaps: Rate-limit key uses unverified x-session-id header, which a client can rotate to bypass per-client limits
No evidence of a shared rate-limit store (e.g. Redis) for multi-replica deployments; default express-rate-limit memory store is per-process
verdicts.remediation: In server/src/index.ts, key the chatLimiter on the verified session identity (e.g. the sid claim after sessionAuth, or a hash of the x-session-token) with req.ip as fallback, and ensure trust proxy is configured correctly so req.ip reflects the real client. If more than one replica runs, back express-rate-limit with a shared store (e.g. rate-limit-redis). Optionally add an ingress-level limit (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rpm) in infra/k8s/ingress.yaml as a defence-in-depth layer.

verdicts.rationale: E1 is a repository document (docs/incident-response.md) that covers the three required elements: detection (alerts on harmful-reply classifier hits, handover-rate spikes, complaints tagged ai-answer), escalation (Customer Care lead and #supportbot-incidents, plus a containment step via the chat.ai_enabled flag), and reporting. Its reporting step requires serious incidents such as harmful or discriminatory output and personal data leaks through the model to be sent to ai-incidents@acme.example within 24 hours, which matches POL-10(2). E2 places the docs/ folder in the repository layout, which supports that the procedure is maintained in the repo. The deterministic pattern check also matches the ai-incidents@ address in E1.
gaps: E1 states the 24-hour deadline without saying it runs from detection
Detection does not explicitly name significant performance degradation or safety events as incident categories
verdicts.remediation: Optionally tighten docs/incident-response.md step 4 to say "within 24 hours of detection" and add explicit detection triggers for significant performance degradation and safety events. No change is required for the current statement to be met.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

evidence.snippet:
# Model card: SupportBot answer generation

* **Provider / model:** OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini` (API, EU data residency), pinned via `LLM_MODEL`.
* **Owner:** Customer Care Engineering (care-eng@acme.example).
* **Intended use:** answering customer questions on orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs using
  retrieved help-centre extracts; handing over to a human agent.
* **Out of scope:** legal, financial or energy-saving advice; contract changes; complaints decisions.
* **Product evaluation (2026-08, 600 labelled conversations):** answer correctness 91.3%, grounded
  in retrieved context 95.0%, correct handover 88.0%, harmful/off-policy replies 0.3%.
* **Limitations:** may hallucinate tariff details not in the help centre; English and German only.

# Privacy notice: support chat

**Controller:** ACME Home Energy GmbH, Hauptstr. 5, 10115 Berlin. DPO: privacy@acme-energy.example.

**Purpose and legal basis.** We process your chat messages to answer your support request
(Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR, performance of your contract) and to improve answer quality and handle
complaints (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, legitimate interest).

**AI assistant.** Replies are generated by an AI assistant operated on our behalf by OpenAI Ireland
Ltd. (processor). You can ask for a human agent at any time.

**Recipients.** OpenAI (processor, EU region), our customer-care team.

**Retention.** Chat transcripts are stored for 2 years and then deleted automatically.

**Your rights.** Right of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, portability and
the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. Contact privacy@acme-energy.example.

# SupportBot

Customer-support assistant for the ACME Home Energy web shop. The widget answers questions about
orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs using an LLM (OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`) grounded on our help
centre articles, and hands over to a human agent on request.

## AI Act position
SupportBot is a chatbot that interacts directly with customers. It does not take decisions about
people and is not in any Annex III area, so it is a **limited-risk** system: the transparency
obligations of Art. 50 apply (users must know they are talking to an AI).

## Layout
| Path | |
|---|---|
| `server/` | Express + TypeScript API (`/api/chat`, admin transcript tools) |
| `web/` | Chat widget (React) embedded in the shop |
| `config/app.yaml` | rate limits, retention, model settings |
| `infra/` | Terraform (RDS Postgres) and Kubernetes manifests |
| `docs/` | privacy notice, record of processing, incident response, ADRs |

# Record of processing activities: SupportBot (entry PA-CC-07)

| Item | Content |
|---|---|
| Controller | ACME Home Energy GmbH; DPO privacy@acme-energy.example |
| Purposes | Customer support via chat; quality assurance; complaint handling |
| Data subjects | Customers and prospective customers using the chat |
| Personal data | Chat messages (free text, may contain contact and contract data), customer id, session id |
| Recipients | Customer-care team; OpenAI Ireland Ltd. (processor) |
| Transfers | None outside the EEA (EU data residency contract) |
| Erasure time limits | Transcripts 2 years; application logs 90 days |
| Security measures | TLS, KMS-encrypted RDS, admin RBAC, rate limiting |

port: 8080
llm:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o-mini
public_endpoints:
  - /api/chat
rate_limit:
  chat_per_minute: 20
retention:
  transcript_days: 730     # 2 years: QA sampling and complaint handling
logging:
  sink: loki
  retention_days: 90

resource "aws_kms_key" "supportbot" {
  description         = "SupportBot data key"
  enable_key_rotation = true
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "transcripts" {
  identifier                 = "supportbot-transcripts"
  engine                     = "postgres"
  engine_version             = "16.3"
  instance_class             = "db.t4g.medium"
  allocated_storage          = 100
  storage_encrypted          = true
  kms_key_id                 = aws_kms_key.supportbot.arn
  db_subnet_group_name       = "private-data"
  publicly_accessible        = false
  backup_retention_period    = 7
  deletion_protection        = true
  parameter_group_name       = "postgres16-force-ssl"
}

# ADR 0001: Use a hosted LLM with retrieval instead of fine-tuning

* Status: accepted (2026-02-11)

We use OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini` through the API with EU data residency and zero data retention on the
provider side, grounded with help-centre extracts (top-4 BM25 + embeddings). Fine-tuning was
rejected: help-centre content changes weekly. Customer messages are sent to the provider as typed;
redaction of contact details was evaluated but postponed because it reduced answer quality for
delivery questions.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: supportbot
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [support-api.acme-energy.example]
      secretName: supportbot-tls
  rules:
    - host: support-api.acme-energy.example
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api/chat
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: {service: {name: supportbot, port: {number: 8080}}}

# AI incident response

1. **Detect:** alerts on harmful-reply classifier hits, spikes in handover rate, customer complaints
   tagged `ai-answer`.
2. **Contain:** on-call engineer can switch the widget to "human agents only" via the feature flag
   `chat.ai_enabled`.
3. **Escalate:** notify Customer Care lead and #supportbot-incidents.
4. **Report:** serious incidents (harmful or discriminatory output, personal data leak through the
   model) are reported to the AI Governance Board at ai-incidents@acme.example within 24 hours;
   personal data breaches also go to the DPO for the 72-hour GDPR assessment.
5. **Review:** blameless post-mortem within 10 working days.
